title: Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
content:
Computer Science > Computation and Language
  [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026]
Title:Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at this https URL.

report.summary: QGPM is a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance to reduce lost-in-the-middle failures in long-context LLMs.
report.background: Long-context language models are increasingly used for document QA, retrieval-augmented generation, codebase analysis, and agent memory, but they often neglect evidence placed in the middle of long inputs. This 'lost-in-the-middle' effect is partly linked to rotary position embedding (RoPE): its long-range decay weakens positional signals between distant tokens. Existing fixes have trade-offs. Input compression deletes low-importance tokens and can remove useful evidence. Attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has already weakened positional signals. RoPE-level remapping modifies positions directly but typically applies the same transformation to every query, ignoring what the user is actually asking. QGPM addresses this by using the model's own attention heads to build query-specific relevance maps and modulate RoPE positions at inference time, without retraining.
key_points: QGPM is training-free: it does not retrain or fine-tune the model. Instead, it uses query relevance signals from the model's own attention heads to reshape RoPE positions during inference. This makes it attractive for existing long-context deployments where retraining would be expensive or impractical.

The method uses two relevance regimes. Lower layers build a broad relevance map, while upper layers build a sharper one. On fast-rotating RoPE planes, low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position, pulling relevant evidence closer to the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout so every token stays in place.

Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER across multiple context lengths show QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines. The largest gains appear on retrieval tasks, where finding specific evidence in long inputs is critical. Results also generalize across multiple model backbones, suggesting the approach is not tied to one architecture.

The work targets a key limitation of prior methods: input compression can delete useful tokens, attention reweighting happens after RoPE weakening, and existing RoPE-level remapping is query-agnostic. QGPM instead makes positional modulation query-dependent, aligning the positional signal with the information the current query needs.
report.impact: QGPM points to a practical inference-time path for improving long-context reliability without retraining. For the AI industry, it strengthens the case that positional encoding, not just context-window size, is a key bottleneck for long-context performance. For developers, the method could be integrated into serving stacks and RAG pipelines to improve retrieval and document QA, especially where evidence is buried mid-context. For regular users, the payoff would be more consistent answers from long PDFs, contracts, codebases, and chat histories, with less dependence on where information happens to appear. The main caveat is that gains are benchmark-dependent and must be validated on real workloads before production deployment.
report.tools: Start with the paper's linked QGPM code release and reproduce results on NoLiMa and RULER. For integration experiments, use Hugging Face Transformers or vLLM with RoPE-based long-context models, and compare against attention-reweighting and input-compression baselines. Track LongRoPE-style position remapping and long-context retrieval benchmarks; validate on your own RAG and document-QA workloads before deployment.
